content: Hot flushes and night sweats are common symptoms experienced by menopausal women. Hormone therapy (HT), which includes either oestrogens alone or a combination of oestrogens and progestogens in a cyclic or continuous regimen, is frequently recommended to alleviate these symptoms. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of oral hormone therapy compared to placebo on vasomotor symptoms, such as hot flushes and night sweats, as well as the risk of early-onset side effects. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Menstrual Disorders and Subfertility Group trials register in May 2002. This register is maintained through regular searches of databases such as MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and PsycINFO. It also includes handsearching of 20 relevant journals, conference proceedings, and key grey literature sources. Additionally, pharmaceutical companies, The Journal of the International Menopause Society, and the journal Climacteric were contacted for relevant data. The study included double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials of oral hormone therapy lasting at least three months. The quality of the studies and the outcome data were independently assessed. Random effects models were used to account for variations in trial methodologies. The meta-analyses were further examined for sensitivity to trial quality and therapy duration. The frequency and severity of symptoms were analyzed separately, along with data on participant withdrawals and side effects. Frequency data were analyzed using the Weighted Mean Difference (WMD) between treatment and placebo outcomes, while severity data were assessed using odds ratios derived from the proportional odds model. Out of 115 references initially identified, 24 trials met the selection criteria and were included in the review. These trials involved a total of 3,329 participants, with study durations ranging from three months to three years. The results showed a significant reduction in the weekly frequency of hot flushes for participants receiving hormone therapy compared to those on placebo. The Weighted Mean Difference (WMD) was -17.92 (95% CI -22.86 to -12.99), which corresponds to a 75% reduction in hot flush frequency (95% CI 64.3% to 82.3%) for hormone therapy relative to placebo. Symptom severity was also significantly reduced in the hormone therapy group compared to placebo, with an odds ratio (OR) of 0.13 (95% CI 0.07 to 0.23). Participants receiving placebo were significantly more likely to withdraw from the study due to lack of efficacy, with an odds ratio of 10.51 (95% CI 5.00 to 22.09). However, withdrawal due to adverse events, such as breast tenderness, oedema, joint pain, and psychological symptoms, was not significantly higher in the hormone therapy group (OR 1.25, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.90). Nonetheless, the overall occurrence of adverse events was significantly increased in the hormone therapy group, with an odds ratio of 1.41 (95% CI 1.00 to 1.99). Interestingly, women in the placebo group experienced a 57.7% reduction in hot flushes (95% CI 45.1% to 67.7%) between baseline and the end of the study, highlighting the substantial placebo effect observed in these trials. The authors concluded that oral hormone therapy is highly effective in reducing hot flushes and night sweats. They emphasized the importance of evaluating therapies for menopausal symptoms in blinded trials against placebo or validated treatments, given the significant placebo effect observed in well-conducted randomized controlled trials. Additionally, menopausal symptoms may naturally fluctuate and often decline after menopause, which further underscores the need for rigorous study designs. Withdrawals due to side effects were only slightly increased in the hormone therapy groups, despite the inability to customize hormone therapy doses in these fixed-dose trials. Future comparisons of hormonal doses, product types, or regimens should focus on trials specifically designed to evaluate these within-study differences.
